units.text: Riverton University invites teams to design a practical improvement for a small community institution. The institution has limited money, uncertain demand, and a responsibility to serve residents fairly. Your proposal should identify one operational problem, explain why existing practices are inadequate, and recommend an intervention that can be tested within one academic term. State the assumptions behind your analysis and explain which observations would cause you to change your recommendation. Include a way to measure progress without collecting unnecessary personal information. Discuss an implementation risk, a possible unintended consequence, and a low cost method for gathering feedback. The evaluation panel values clear reasoning over ambitious technology. Teams may use simple schedules, physical tools, or public information where appropriate. Do not assume that additional staff, permanent subsidies, or expensive equipment will become available. Conclude by explaining how the institution could decide whether to continue, adapt, or stop the proposed pilot after review.

units.text:
A queue works best when arrivals can see how service order is decided. Numbered tickets
separate a visitor's place in line from the place where that visitor stands. This lets people sit, read,
or wait in shade without losing their turn. The organiser should announce exceptions openly and
keep an accessible route to the service desk. A ticket system does not create more service
capacity; it only makes the existing waiting process easier to understand.

units.text: Riverton University invites teams to design a practical improvement for a small community institution. The institution has limited money, uncertain demand, and a responsibility to serve residents fairly. Your proposal should identify one operational problem, explain why existing practices are inadequate, and recommend an intervention that can be tested within one academic term. State the assumptions behind your analysis and explain which observations would cause you to change your recommendation. Include a way to measure progress without collecting unnecessary personal information. Discuss an implementation risk, a possible unintended consequence, and a low cost method for gathering feedback. The evaluation panel values clear reasoning over ambitious technology. Teams may use simple schedules, physical tools, or public information where appropriate. Do not assume that additional staff, permanent subsidies, or expensive equipment will become available. Conclude by explaining how the institution could decide whether to continue, adapt, or stop the proposed pilot after review.

The community bakery discards unsold bread at closing, but baking less every day could leave weekend customers empty handed. I propose a two colour chalkboard tally of early and late sales. The baker can record loaves by product without linking purchases to individual customers. After a fortnight, dough batches for slow weekday afternoons can be reduced while weekend production remains unchanged.

Weather and a neighbouring school holiday could distort the short trial, so the tally should include those circumstances in a margin note. Donating edible leftovers must remain an option while production is adjusted. A reduction in waste accompanied by repeated stockouts would count as failure, because discarded weight alone rewards underproduction. The baker should compare both leftovers and unfilled requests before continuing. Feedback can come from a small basket of paper comments near the counter. The proposed intervention is a production scheduling change that uses equipment already present in the shop.

A robotics workshop can teach children to sort coloured blocks by writing simple rules on paper. The session uses cardboard pieces instead of expensive motors. Volunteers can count how many rule cards lead to the intended arrangement. No account registration is needed, and each child can take home the instructions after the exercise. The organiser will compare different teaching sequences during the following school term.

A municipal choir wants to choose a rehearsal venue with a comfortable acoustic response. Singers will perform the same melody in three borrowed rooms while listeners record which words remain understandable. Heavy curtains may reduce troublesome echoes. The committee should compare the notes before renting a permanent hall, because low rent alone cannot compensate for severe reverberation. The final decision will include travel time from nearby bus stops.
